bib.title: A comprehensive taxonomy of hallucinations in Large Language Models

legacy_report:
COVERAGE: 55 of 55 pages extracted (139,016 chars). I read the front matter, sections 1-2, 3.2, 4.4-4.6, 6.2, all of 7, 8.1-8.1.3, 9.2, 9.4 and 10 in full. I skimmed the rest (Table 1-3 text, sections 5, 6.3-6.5, 8.2-8.3, the other 9.x sections, references). I did not open the figure images. I did not run figures.py.

SOURCE: "A comprehensive taxonomy of hallucinations in Large Language Models", Manuel Cossio (MMed, MEng), single author, Universitat de Barcelona. The stamp reads arXiv:2508.01781v1 [cs.CL], 3 Aug 2025. No venue is stated, so treat it as a preprint.

CORE CLAIM: This is a survey and taxonomy report with no experiments of its own. It sorts hallucination into intrinsic vs extrinsic and factuality vs faithfulness, then lists manifestations, causes, evaluation metrics and mitigations. Its thesis is that hallucination is inevitable in any computable LLM, so the goal should shift from elimination to detection, mitigation and human oversight.

HEADLINE NUMBERS (none are the paper's own measurements; all are quoted from other work and the paper gives no setup for them):
- Logical inconsistencies are 19% of "identified hallucination cases". Quote: "accounts for a notable portion, specifically 19%, of identified hallucination cases [42;47;34;95]" (sec 4.4, p.12). The paper does not say which sample.
- Temporal disorientation is 12%. Quote: "This category accounts for 12% of identified hallucination cases.[47;51]" (sec 4.5).
- Ethical violations are 6%. Quote: "Ethical violations represent 6% of hallucination cases in some analyses. [47;40;31]" (sec 4.6).
- Treat these three as unverifiable without checking refs 34, 42, 47, 51, 95.
- Other numbers ("~70% of prompts each month are fresh", ">40% of battles involving an open model" for LM Arena) are quoted from the LM Arena site and are not hallucination results.

NOVEL VS RESTATED: Almost nothing is new.
- The inevitability theorems (Theorems 1-3, Corollary 1, diagonalization) restate Xu et al., "Hallucination is Inevitable: An Innate Limitation of Large Language Models" (ref [100]; the text names the paper but not its authors or year). They are in sec 2.2 and Table 1.
- The intrinsic/extrinsic and factuality/faithfulness splits restate refs [38], [7], [70], [79] and others. The paper itself says several overlapping taxonomies exist.
- The metrics and benchmarks (TruthfulQA, HalluLens, FactScore, Q2/QuestEval, FactCC, SummaC, KILT, RAGAS) are summarised from their own papers.
- The only candidates for new content are the organising synthesis: Table 2 (taxonomy), Table 3 (causes) and the section 9 tour of web dashboards (Artificial Analysis, Vectara leaderboard, Epoch AI, LM Arena, with screenshots from 28-29 June 2025). These are descriptions, not findings.

QUOTES:
1. p.7: "the focus must pivot towards designing systems that incorporate robust detection mechanisms, containment strategies, and, crucially, human-in-the-loop validation".
2. p.31: "Despite its advantages, RAG is not foolproof: the model may still hallucinate if it fails to properly interpret or align with the retrieved material [90]."
3. p.27, on Retrieval-Augmented Evaluation (RAE): it checks "whether the evidence retrieved by a RAG system genuinely supports the claims made in the generated output", in two steps: identify the claims, then verify each against the retrieved snippets. The sources are [48;84;28;85], which include the RAGAS paper by Es et al. and Salemi & Zamani on retrieval-quality evaluation.

LIMITS:
- It has no experiments, no ablations and no RAG-specific measurements.
- The author concedes the lack of a standard hallucination definition (7.3.1), task dependence of metrics (7.3.2), insensitivity to subtle errors such as altered numbers or dates (7.3.3), and scores that give no diagnosis (7.3.4).
- The inevitability result holds only in a formal world of computable ground-truth functions and does not predict real-world rates.
- It also claims RAG helps mainly with extrinsic hallucinations and that intrinsic ones need consistency checks, with no evidence given.
- Several benchmark descriptions look doubtful and I did not verify them. For example, FactScore is described as an entailment-based summarization benchmark, and HalluLens as annotated with severity. This is from my own recollection, not the PDF. Do not cite those descriptions without checking the original papers.
- The leaderboard screenshots (Vectara, Fig 8) are dated June 2025 and have no numbers in the text.

BUILDS ON: Xu et al. (ref 100), the surveys [38], [42], [47], Toolformer [86], Lewis et al. and Izacard & Grave for RAG ([48], [39]), RAGAS [28], SummaC [45], FactCC [44], and Q2 [37].

BEST-FIT NOTE SECTION: "Faithful is not correct" (line 150) and the "Faithfulness: claim by claim" grounding tiers (lines 111-125). The paper's faithfulness/factuality and intrinsic/extrinsic split and its RAE two-step description fit there. "Pitfalls" is the second choice, for the "RAG is not foolproof" caveat. This is a sharpens-level citation at best. Add it to references.md as a taxonomy and definition source, not as evidence.

FIGURE: none that explains the claim. Fig 8 (p.37) is a Vectara leaderboard screenshot ("grounded hallucinations rate using Hughes hallucination evaluation model, retrieved on 29 June 2025"), but it is a dated dashboard capture and not a result of the paper.

PROBLEMS: None. The extraction was clean and I found no embedded instructions. Table text on pp.8-9 and 13-14 may be partly flattened.
